scenes.visual: Title card 'Keeping the Gas Fresh' fades in over the alveolus sac and tube from the first film, 16:9. Same colour map as the first film. COLOUR MAP, same in every scene and in the second film: water or air = BLUE arrows and BLUE stream; blood = RED arrows and RED stream; oxygen = small GOLD dots riding in each stream, their density showing the oxygen partial pressure within that stream only (dense = high, sparse = low), with the PO2 value as on-screen text; dot density never stands for total oxygen per litre, which appears only as a separate 'oxygen per litre' bar; carbon dioxide = small PURPLE dots; diffusion across the barrier = thin GOLD arrows for oxygen, PURPLE arrows for carbon dioxide; the barrier = a GREY strip. Labels on screen use the symbols PO2, PCO2, deltaP (shown as the Greek capital delta then P), A, T. Cartoon schematics only, no molecular structures; any curve or bar not computed is labelled 'schematic'. Numbers appear only as on-screen text. Added for this film: the airway tube = GREY outline, the dead-space part of each breath = PALE GREY air, fresh air reaching the sac = bright BLUE.

scenes.tts: Two people move the same total air each minute. So why is one of them building up carbon dioxide while the other is not?
scenes.visual: Two cartoon people side by side, each with a counter reading 'air moved: 6 L per minute'. Over the right-hand person a PURPLE gauge labelled 'PCO2' creeps upward. Question card: 'Same air moved. Why more carbon dioxide?'
scenes.narration: Two people move the same total air each minute. So why is one of them building up carbon dioxide while the other is not?

scenes.tts: The first film ended at a dead-ended sac, the alveolus. Blood can at best match the gas inside it. Blood flow keeps bringing new blood. But the gas must be renewed too, through the airways. So what keeps moving fresh air in?
scenes.visual: Recall the first film's alveolus: the round sac on its tube, RED capillaries wrapped round it, the exit gauge stopping at the alveolar line. RED blood streams on through the capillaries (label: 'blood flow renews the blood'), while the sac's gas pales (label: 'the gas must be renewed too'). Caption card: 'blood matches the gas it last touches: what keeps that gas fresh?'
scenes.narration: The first film ended at a dead-ended sac, the alveolus. Blood can at best match the gas inside it. Blood flow keeps bringing new blood. But the gas must be renewed too, through the airways. So what keeps moving fresh air in?

scenes.tts: A mammal pulls air in. The diaphragm, a dome of muscle under the lungs, contracts and flattens. The chest enlarges, pressure in the lungs falls, and air flows in. This is aspiration.
scenes.visual: Block-schematic chest: a domed diaphragm under the lung flattens downward; the chest outline widens; a pressure gauge inside the lung dips below a line labelled 'outside air pressure'; BLUE arrows flow in through the mouth and down the tube. Label: 'aspiration'.
scenes.narration: A mammal pulls air in. The diaphragm, a dome of muscle under the lungs, contracts and flattens. The chest enlarges, pressure in the lungs falls, and air flows in. This is aspiration.

scenes.tts: But a tube leads to the sac. The airways, from nose and mouth down to the smallest bronchioles with no alveoli, exchange nothing. They are dead space.
scenes.visual: Zoom to the airway tube from nose and mouth down to a fine branch, outlined in GREY and labelled 'dead space: conducting airways, no exchange'. The sac at the end is labelled 'alveoli'.
scenes.narration: But a tube leads to the sac. The airways, from nose and mouth down to the smallest bronchioles with no alveoli, exchange nothing. They are dead space.

scenes.tts: So the first air into the sac each breath is stale air left in the tube. And fresh air still in the tube when you stop breathing in is breathed out unused.
scenes.visual: One inhalation animates: a PALE GREY slug of stale air enters the sac first, followed by bright BLUE fresh air. On the exhale, bright BLUE air left in the tube is pushed back out the mouth, labelled 'breathed out unused'.
scenes.narration: So the first air into the sac each breath is stale air left in the tube. And fresh air still in the tube when you stop breathing in is breathed out unused.

scenes.tts: Take slow, deep breaths. Each breath clears the dead space and sends a large fresh portion into the sac. The total air moved each minute is minute ventilation. The fresh part reaching the alveoli is alveolar ventilation.
scenes.visual: Repeated slow, deep breaths: each one pushes the PALE GREY slug through and a big bright BLUE portion into the sac. A counter labelled 'alveolar ventilation (fresh air reaching alveoli per minute)' fills to a high mark; a second counter 'minute ventilation (total air moved)' sits beside it.
scenes.narration: Take slow, deep breaths. Each breath clears the dead space and sends a large fresh portion into the sac. The total air moved each minute is minute ventilation. The fresh part reaching the alveoli is alveolar ventilation.

scenes.tts: Now keep the total air per minute the same, but take smaller, faster breaths. Does carbon dioxide in the sac rise, fall or stay the same?
scenes.visual: Breathing switches to quick, shallow breaths. The 'minute ventilation' counter stays at the same mark. The PURPLE PCO2 gauge in the sac is covered by a question mark. Question card: 'Same total air, smaller breaths: alveolar carbon dioxide?'
scenes.narration: Now keep the total air per minute the same, but take smaller, faster breaths. Does carbon dioxide in the sac rise, fall or stay the same?

scenes.visual: Question card holds over the shallow-breathing sac; a small timer ring fills.

scenes.tts: It rises. Each small breath barely clears the dead space. Less fresh air reaches the sac, while the body makes carbon dioxide as fast as before.
scenes.visual: Each shallow breath pushes mostly PALE GREY stale air into the sac, with only a thin BLUE sliver. The 'alveolar ventilation' counter drops while 'minute ventilation' holds steady. PURPLE dots pour into the sac from the capillaries at the same rate as before and pile up; the PCO2 gauge climbs. Label: 'carbon dioxide production unchanged (schematic)'.
scenes.narration: It rises. Each small breath barely clears the dead space. Less fresh air reaches the sac, while the body makes carbon dioxide as fast as before.

scenes.tts: Here the first film's rule runs in reverse. Blood giving up carbon dioxide leaves with no lower partial pressure than the gas it last touched. So the blood's carbon dioxide climbs with the sac's.
scenes.visual: The RED capillary leaving the sac carries PURPLE dots; its PCO2 gauge is linked by a dashed line to the sac's PCO2 gauge and rises with it. Label: 'blood leaving tracks alveolar PCO2'.
scenes.narration: Here the first film's rule runs in reverse. Blood giving up carbon dioxide leaves with no lower partial pressure than the gas it last touched. So the blood's carbon dioxide climbs with the sac's.

scenes.tts: The brainstem watches that result. Carbon dioxide crosses into the brain's fluid and lowers its P H. Sensors near the brainstem surface detect the fall, and the drive to breathe rises.
scenes.caption: The brainstem watches that result. Carbon dioxide crosses into the brain's fluid and lowers its pH. Sensors near the brainstem surface detect the fall, and the drive to breathe rises.
scenes.visual: Cut to a cartoon brainstem. PURPLE dots cross a GREY wall labelled 'blood-brain barrier' into the fluid around it; a 'pH' gauge in the fluid dips. Small sensor blocks on the brainstem surface, labelled 'central chemoreceptors', light up; a 'drive to breathe' arrow runs down to the diaphragm and thickens.
scenes.narration: The brainstem watches that result. Carbon dioxide crosses into the brain's fluid and lowers its pH. Sensors near the brainstem surface detect the fall, and the drive to breathe rises.

scenes.tts: Haldane and Priestley sampled the last of a forced breath out. In resting subjects, a small rise in alveolar carbon dioxide greatly increased breathing. Lowering oxygen did little until it fell far.
scenes.visual: A cartoon subject at rest breathes out hard through a long tube; the last portion is caught in a sample bag labelled 'end of forced breath = alveolar sample'. Credit text: 'J. S. Haldane and J. G. Priestley, 1905'. Two schematic arrows, labelled 'schematic': 'small rise in alveolar CO2' leads to a big 'ventilation' bar; 'oxygen lowered' leads to a barely changed bar until a far-off point marked 'falls far'.
scenes.narration: Haldane and Priestley sampled the last of a forced breath out. In resting subjects, a small rise in alveolar carbon dioxide greatly increased breathing. Lowering oxygen did little until it fell far.

scenes.tts: So breathing keeps the gas the blood touches fresh. At rest, a mammal's controller mostly reads carbon dioxide. That level is the result of its own breathing, set against the body's carbon dioxide output. Too little fresh air, and carbon dioxide climbs. The sensors then push breathing back up.
scenes.visual: A loop diagram: 'alveolar ventilation' and a second input, 'carbon dioxide production by the body', together set 'alveolar PCO2', which sets 'blood PCO2', which the 'brainstem sensors' read, which sets 'breathing', closing the loop. Small labels: 'resting mammal' and 'steady state, breathing ordinary air'.
scenes.narration: So breathing keeps the gas the blood touches fresh. At rest, a mammal's controller mostly reads carbon dioxide. That level is the result of its own breathing, set against the body's carbon dioxide output. Too little fresh air, and carbon dioxide climbs. The sensors then push breathing back up.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'At fixed CO2 output, alveolar ventilation, not total air, sets alveolar PCO2.' Small scope line beneath it: 'steady state, breathing ordinary air'.
